more_beautiful.reason: B has a richer, more polished visual system: a luggage-tag hero, a warm and controlled palette, strong slab-serif hierarchy, and consistent cards and chips. A is tidy but sparse, with a lopsided desktop hero and flat mint and grey blocks.

less_generic.reason: A carries one idea all the way through: the raffle or cloakroom ticket shows up in the wordmark, the arrival slots and the generated booking, and there are no stock landing-page sections. Apart from its luggage tag, B relies on familiar template patterns: an eyebrow label, a two-tone headline, icon feature cards, a numbered 'How it works' and a three-column footer.

better_overall.reason: B is more complete and more inviting. Visitors can pick from several dates, send a prefilled email in one tap with a copy fallback, and find the venue and contact details. The owner gets a setup note and an optional form backend. Its invented phone number, placeholder address and made-up policies must still be fixed before launch.

A: The next date sits in the H1 with a highlight. It is calculated automatically, rolls forward after 1pm on the day, and the owner can list dates to skip
One ticket idea links the wordmark, the half-hour slot tickets and the generated booking ticket, and it speaks directly to the 'don't all turn up at 10' problem
The form is very accessible: an error summary with jump links, inline errors, aria-invalid and aria-describedby, whole-ticket tap targets, and high contrast (7:1 on the button)
It is honest: no invented address, phone number or policies, a plain 'This is not a booking yet' message, and a copy-text fallback for people without an email app
The copy is short and plain, with useful fault examples and a reminder to bring the charger or cable
B: The luggage-tag hero shows the date with a live 'Tomorrow' / 'In N days' label, plus the hours, last arrivals and the venue
The visual system is polished and consistent: a warm palette, a clear slab-serif hierarchy, and cards, chips and buttons that match at both 375 and 1280 px

The booking flow does more: a choice of the next three Saturdays, icon chips, email or phone for confirmation, a prefilled email in one tap, a copy fallback, an optional form-service endpoint, a honeypot spam trap, and 'Book another item'
The owner sees a note flagging the placeholder email until it is changed, and without JavaScript the page still reads 'first Saturday of every month'
There is practical visitor content: bring items clean and with chargers, how a session works, find us, help with access, and a call for volunteers

A: The desktop hero is sparse and lopsided, with a large empty right side, and the flat mint and grey bands look unfinished
Booking takes two steps (get the ticket, then email it), and the 'Get your ticket' button could be mistaken for a confirmed booking
The page gives no location beyond 'the church hall' and no contact route. The placeholder booking email only appears after a visitor creates a ticket, so the owner may never notice it
The fallback date is hardcoded in the HTML and will go out of date if the script fails. Only the next session can be booked
B: It presents invented facts as real: a phone number you can tap to call (01632 960123), a placeholder street address and Maps link, and made-up policies ('later slots are usually quieter', drop-ins welcome, one item per booking, no volunteers for phones or laptops)
It widens the 'can fix' list beyond what the owner said (kettles, radios, hairdryers, soft toys)
Much of the structure is template-like: an eyebrow label, a two-tone headline, icon feature cards, a numbered 'How it works' section and a three-column footer
On a phone the large tag pushes the intro and main call to action well below the fold, and the page is long
The organiser setup note is visible to the public until someone edits the file
